title: Remote Control Conceptual Design Meeting
summary: The team held a conceptual design meeting to discuss features and components for a new TV remote control targeted at young professionals. They reviewed market research highlighting a demand for fancy aesthetics and technological innovation, as well as fashion trends favoring spongy materials and vibrant fruit colors. Technical discussions covered battery options, printed circuit boards, casing materials, and display interfaces. The group agreed on a flip-top design featuring a plastic inner case, a detachable spongy rubber outer cover, kinetic charging, an LCD touch display, and rubber buttons.
topics: Voice recognition and remote locator feature
decisions: Adopt kinetic charging powered by a watch-type battery cell.
Design a flip-top remote with a plastic inner shell and a detachable spongy rubber outer cover.
Use fruit and vegetable-inspired vibrant colors for the rubber outer cover.
Implement a black-and-white LCD touch display on the top inner panel.
Place rubber anti-RSI buttons for channel and volume control on the bottom inner panel.
Incorporate a voice recognition locator feature (or whistle locator as a backup) pending cost evaluation.

actions.task: Check the financial feasibility and cost of incorporating the voice recognition locator feature.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Welcome back, everybody. Hope you had fun. Right, this is our conceptual design meeting. I think we're slightly ahead of ourselves from the last meeting.

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah, I was getting that impression as well.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: I think, yeah. This is where we talk about properties, materials, user interface, and trend watching. So, I think we've touched on a few things to do with that already, but we'll just go over it. The minutes from last time, we had a couple of changes in our plans in that we couldn't use teletext, it wasn't going to be a control for everything, and that we had to incorporate the image of the company into it somehow. We have decided on leaving out the voice recognition. We've decided on there being a flip design and a different shape from what's normal. We were thinking a shell, but something along those lines, just a different shape from what's normal. You were going to look into there being rechargeable batteries...

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: ...and we're going to think about the port and an alarm for getting it lost, things like that. And our market was going to be young, business kind of range. Okay, so should we start with the first presentation?

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Shall I?

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Yes, if you feel.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: We'll just connect up. Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Okay, so we decided on our market, and so this feedback from the marketing department is really about trend watching. The methods we used to decide on current trends and so on, market trends, were that we did our usual market research study with our 100 subjects. And the general feedback from them is that the most... I'm sorry, I'm slightly tongue-tied after lunch, sorry, project manager! We decided on the most important aspect required in a remote control device, and we'll come to that later. So that was one of the first things we did. Also, with our company being forerunners in putting fashion into technology, we also looked at a fashion update using our consultants on fashion and design in Paris and Milan. So the general findings from that were that in the market trends, the most important aspects for remote controls were: people want a fancy look and feel rather than the current functional look and feel of remote controls. They also want a remote control to be technologically innovative, and of course, as we predicted, that it should be easy to use. Now I should point out that the first of those findings, fancy look and feel, is the most important—it's twice as important as the second, technologically innovative, which is in turn twice as important as being easy to use. So possibly that the feature that we put first is actually third. It's still important, but it's third in order of preference for the subjects that we looked at. Okay. Now the fashion update, which relates to very personal preferences among our subject group, we found from our consultants in Paris and Milan, who attended all the design and fashion fairs there, that fruit and vegetables are going to be the theme for clothes, shoes, and furniture. So should we be thinking of using something like that in our remote control design, too? There also seems to be a trend towards a spongy feel to materials, again in contrast to last year. So a lot of interesting feedback there, both from our market research department and from our people in Paris and Milan. Be interesting to see what our design people make of that.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Okay, thank you very much. Let's start from the inside and work our way out, unless anyone has any questions about that? Not yet? Okay.

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yes, thank you.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: I hate those little things. Especially if you do them on too tight and you can't get the leverage on them to undo them.

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Okay, this is all about the design of the inner components and the availability of the components we have in stock at the moment. First, into the method. The main idea of the whole thing is just so you press buttons and it should activate things on the TV, and we discussed last meeting that it should be easy to find. Also in this study, I've looked into the availability of some of the materials, because some of the things that we looked at last time aren't, unfortunately, available. Findings: I've got my nice little picture there. This is the chip called the TA11835, which is what's used in pretty much every remote control because it sends out standard signals based on your input, and it's pretty much used for all TV remotes at the moment. And then we're looking into battery options. There's actually no rechargeable option available. So I saw the standard AA and AAA, which we thought were a bit too bulky at the moment. Dynamo charging, I thought that might be a bit silly, to be honest—basically like wind-up radio. So you wind up your remote control before you use it.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: How long can you get out of that? I mean, can you pick it up and then wind it for two minutes, and then that's it for the night, or...?

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah, I presume you wouldn't have to wind it for very long, but I don't think it's really necessary when you think of the next two options, like solar charging, because most people have the light on in the room anyway, so they could get...

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Does that light charge as sunlight does, artificial light?

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Is it? Oh, right.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: Regarding the sizes, which one do you think will be like, because we have to take into consideration size also. So maybe standard AAA might take less space, and dynamo might take most...

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah, it would. Yeah, the dynamo would take more space because you'd actually need a physical sort of handle to wind up.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: I'm pretty sure that solar is from the sun. Yeah, I don't think it counts artificial light, no. But I mean, you don't want to limit your market. I mean, people who live in basement flats, there's not that many people, but there are people.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: In different parts of the world, too, if we're marketing internationally.

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah, most people also watch TV in the night anyway.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: But then it would be charging through the day. I think the point is that it charges through the day and then you've got it charged.

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: But I think the next one's the best anyway: kinetic charging, which is like you get in wristwatches. And you don't even notice it. I mean, the amount of moving around you'd be doing all the time would charge it up. I don't think you'd ever need to actually physically start shaking it up to make it work.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: And what is the life of the kinetic battery? It runs for a long time?

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah, it charges into a smaller cell, which it charges into, the size of a watch battery, because they use them quite frequently in watches. And that would last for... well, I'm not entirely sure how long it would last, but I've never seen one run out.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: But then if you think about a watch, it's on your wrist, so it's on your body the whole time. So you're walking around, you're doing things, it is moving a lot of the time. If you... I mean, you switch the TV on, then you put it on the side, then you pick it up to change it, then you put it on the side...

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah, but then again...

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: ...is it really going to be enough?

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: I think it is, because if you think about it, the watch, although it's only a tiny amount, it's always moving for the whole day, and they don't run out overnight when you leave them on the side. And for the same reason, you're only using it for an incredibly short amount of time just to send a signal, and then you're finished with it.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: So it's not a big draw on it, is it?

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: No, I don't think the draw would be...

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Could I just ask, referring back to solar charging, is that compatible with standard batteries? I mean, could people put standard batteries in, but they could leave it in the sunlight for solar charging, or are the two things not compatible?

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah, you could have a dual power thing, but the thing with the solar cells is you would need to put them on the case, because on a calculator they're quite big and they all look identical.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: So that affects the exterior design.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Expensive as well. What kind of price are we looking at for... I presume normal batteries are the cheapest?

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah, normal batteries would be the cheapest. I presume then it would actually be the solar charging ones. But I think they're not very resistant to dropping. Because if you drop stuff, yeah, the size you'd need to charge a remote wouldn't be that big, but remotes always get thrown around and stuff. So I think, practically...

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Calculators you don't really throw around a lot, whereas remotes you do.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Don't calculators have a battery in them as well?

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah, they do, yeah, they've got dual things, but the batteries are smaller, I think.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: And question is like, sorry, which one would last the longest? Because we don't want customers to be like, you know, charging like a mobile phone every day or remote control like...

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah, so if you had something using the standard batteries and the solar charging, I don't think you'd... well, you know how long the standard AAs would last.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Or would it just detract from the attractiveness of the whole feature? Would it add anything?

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Okay, can we add in an attachment to clothing feature?

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Can we think about that? Because if we're doing the kinetic thing...

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Shouldn't we do some market research on that first before we add it in? Because I personally...

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Well, add it in to think about.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Right, okay.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Because if it is the kinetic thing, and it is small, and it is portable, and it is a different shape, and kinetic is something people don't do, we're doing something original and different. But if you wore it, if it's something you could clip on your pocket, then you would have that less... you wouldn't lose it so much. But then maybe that's looking at someone who's just sitting on their own rather than the eternal battle for control of the remote.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: It's not something that's come up in any of our focus groups and market research. It's not a thing that people are looking for when we threw it open to the field, yeah. But something to put on the side to think about, maybe.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Okay, right.

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Okay, well, I'll move on. My second part of my findings: most current remotes use this silicon PCB board, printed circuit board, which basically has these contacts that are really close together, and then when you press down on the rubber button, it'll connect the circuit, and each switch is connected to two different legs on the chip, and so sends a different message. And that then gets translated by the chip into a code and then it's fired out of this LED in a sequence of on and off bursts.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: What kind of things do we have to consider there? Does it come in varying sizes or is it just one size? And we would have to fit the design...

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Well, the thing about it is they can be as big or small as you want them to be, because you can print a circuit board like that, that it's simply spaced like that so you can fit the size of the nine buttons in. If you see how thin the tracks are, you could put them virtually right next to each other and have a much smaller switch on each one if you wanted to. But there is an option to do it like that, or you could have some sort of array of switches, which I'll speak about in the next bit. So that... and then to conserve battery life, the remote should be in a standby mode while not being used. Now what I was thinking about that was, because sometimes when you have these things, they've got little lights behind the buttons so you can see what all the buttons are, like on a mobile phone they do it more often than on a TV remote, but you could have lights behind the buttons, and after like 5 or 10 seconds of not being used, I'd have that turned off if we decided to go for buttons that could light up.

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: The case material: I've been sent what the factory can actually give us. There's the plastic, which I think we were going to go for anyway, as the main case housing. And the main problems with... well, you could go for wood, but I think it would be a bit impractical. Titanium, very expensive, just the process to make it is expensive. And rubber... well, you were saying that people like this spongy feel this year, so perhaps something made of rubber, but I was thinking more of the buttons, because the buttons which they've said that they've put across are what is used in some stress-ball manufacture, and it's meant to be anti-RSI. I'm not sure how that would work, because surely your fingers would still be moving over the short distances, but that's what they said. The problem with the casing is that there's quite a few design restrictions that they've got on the shape of the case. If you go for titanium, they can only do a standard box shape, whereas if you come to plastic, they can be a little more... they can do sort of curved shapes. But whether or not... because we'd have it in two separate units for the flip phone...

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: Yeah. And second question is like, on mobile you can change the cover, call it a skin or whatever. So in this case, if we are looking at like, a customer can change the color, like from parrot green to chili red or something like that? So is that feature available in titanium, or is it only specific to plastic?

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah, in titanium I don't think it would be available at all, really. Just... well, you could make it available in the titanium, it's just it would be so expensive to buy a new case for it because of how much titanium is. It's light and strong, but I think it should be left for aircraft design rather than for a remote.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: It does mark quite easily, too, if you let it fall. I've got a mobile phone myself which is titanium, and it does mark very easily if you drop it.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: I was just wondering, if we make the basic mold out of plastic, but have like a rubber cover that goes over, that would give the spongy feel, that also allows us to kind of have different fashions.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: And you can peel them off, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: So instead of the fascia that comes off being plastic, the fascia that comes off would be the rubber.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Like a rubber sleeve almost, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Like those pens that you get with the grip, that you can pull on and off.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: That could be a good idea, yeah. It would be comfortable to hold on, also.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Very cheap way of changing the look of it, and people can just buy a new one if they want to.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Well, that's been really popular with mobile phones, so I don't see why not.

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Also, just going back to the interface designs with the buttons, we were planning to do some sort of touch screen. Now what I was saying before about, instead of having... you could have just a bare PCB circuit board, and I'm sure you could probably get it in different colors, and so just by touching it with your finger it would make the connection if you had them close enough. That would be one option. The second option, they offer rubber buttons, but I thought that an LCD type of screen, because one, they're incredibly thin and don't take up much space. Two, you can arrange the buttons on the screen in a sort of set thing, and you could have them like a touch display.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: Sorry, I didn't get the last part you were talking of.

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Oh, what...?

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: Just what you said, I didn't get the meaning of it completely.

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Oh, on the LCD screen... The problem with it basically is that it's flat, and so you can't do lots of curved things with it. But you wouldn't have... with the LCD, you'd have the wires coming off, you wouldn't have that with the LCD, you'd only have that with the printed circuit board.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, I don't see why the curved thing is a problem. If we, for example, had the shell, once we open that, yeah, we can have a flat screen inside.

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah, but I'm just wondering whether we want an LCD screen inside. It wouldn't be like full color, it would just be black and white, but there'd be touch buttons, so you wouldn't be pressing down on them. Or we could have rubber buttons which are made of this material which is anti-RSI.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: I think it would be good to have a contrast between, if the whole thing is going to be this rubber thing, it would be good to open it up and see something quite fancy-looking inside. Now how would you distinguish, if you had it bare, how would you distinguish where you had to press?

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah, I hadn't really thought of that.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Here's another idea, I don't know if it helps with that, but just to do with the RSI: is it possible, just as an option, when we open it up, people can use their fingers to press the button, or we have inside like a small pointer thing that people can...

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah, you could have some sort of stylus that you could pull out, but I think they could get a bit easily lost.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Yeah, easy to replace as well.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: Somebody who switches channels very often or does use a particular function very often, he'll find it very irritating to use a, you know...

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: ...and he might spoil the touchpad very fast compared to a button, like if you keep punching with the pointer or whatever.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Yeah, just a thought. They wouldn't actually need one, they could use anything they've got, couldn't they, a pencil, a pen, so they wouldn't really need a...

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Okay, we'll talk about that. So if you finish yours, we'll come back to that.

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah, that's the end.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: One question before your this thing: regarding the circuits, since we are having a flip top, can we customize two circuits for different types of buttons? Like we are keeping the standard buttons on the top, and more complex buttons in this thing, so we can divide the circuit?

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah, that would be fairly simple. I mean, you'd actually have two separate circuit boards, but they'd be joined by wires or like some cabling between them, because in the actual flip bit you'd have some linking.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Just another point occurs to me, kind of applies to both our designers here, I'm not sure how it would fit in. If we flip open, now you know how you've got some mirrors in nightclubs that are mirrors when you turn to them, and you turn away and it gives like an advertising display, you've seen those?

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: And they kind of respond to the turn of your body. Is it possible that when we open our flip-top shell, it's a little compact mirror, and when you press a button, it then goes onto the remote control display thing?

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: We're marketing to guys as much as we are to women.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: They don't look at themselves? Just a thought.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Well, it's a remote control, you're sitting watching TV, are you going to want to open it and see... I know what you mean, because they're using the ideas for mobile phones, they've kind of got sidetracked onto that, I think. Just trying to think of other features we can build in that wouldn't cost too much, but we'll maybe leave that one on the side.

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: I mean, you could do it, you could have a... because if you just put the full charge through an LCD display, it'll completely blank it out, but I don't know if you could get any mirror effect on that.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: I think we'll forget about the mirror, that was just a very quick passing thought, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: Okay, I would like to show something which I did here. First thing is basically on design, we just took the input from the previous meeting, especially from the marketing and industrial design to check on the customer needs and feasibility. Second is we checked into competitors. The picture here shows what are the standard models offered by competitors here. So you generally see there's not much of variety and, like marketing team said, people need trendy, they're bored of black and white. So you generally see rectangular shape, very monotonous kind of designs here. Second thing is, there's too much of confusion here. No particular remote is standard. Like some people have... here, you see this? I found that the only common feature is the channel control and the volume control, rest other buttons they are in a very disorganized way and they are not consistent with other models. Okay, and second, as already discussed with William, we are going to have maybe a GUI interface in the middle of the flip top.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Sorry, what does that stand for?

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: Graphic User Interface, basically which is what we do in computers, have icons or touchpad or whatever.

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: If you have buttons that appear on the screen in this LCD screen...

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: Like you have icons or something you have, it's a good example of GUI, graphic user interface.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: So basically a person need not point or click or press any particular device, he just has to click on that particular icon to simplify it. And on the top, repetitive buttons which are like volume or channel changing and all, could be on the pointing device, that means use of buttons. So he need not use a pointer to keep changing the channel if a person is a frequent surfer. So we are having a combination of both. So on the simpler board on the top, we have these rubber buttons to keep frequently changing the channels.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Can we swap that round? So the ones that we use all the time are on the bottom part? Because if you're thinking about holding it, you would be using your thumbs to press, just like a mobile phone. You'd flip it open and you'd be...

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Wouldn't you? Isn't that the idea? If we just use the shell as an example again, you open that, you've got your LCD display there and you've got the buttons there, so you're holding it...

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: That's what I was just saying. And then have the LCD at the top and then be able to touch that for the other controls. So have the volume and the program, things like that, on the lower side.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: So the findings are: too many cluttered buttons, repetition of certain patterns which I already explained, example the volume and channel control buttons, all are confusing and inconsistent. Okay, we had a latest finding of voice recognition, there was an email which mentioned that our division has developed a new speech recognition feature. We have to check into the financial feasibility whether we can incorporate this at a low cost. But like we had a response from the customers that they would like to have the feature of finding it. So it could be like, 'Where is the remote?' and the remote answers, 'I am here.' Yeah, some kind of thing or it gives a blip sound, some kind of sound. And if this can be incorporated, this would be more trendy also and technologically innovative also. So we can check into the financial feasibility of incorporating this.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: My personal preferences would be like, as already highlighted by marketing department, they want something to do with fruit, so I wouldn't say the design should be like a fruit, but yeah, we can take inspiration from fruit colors, like the vibrant colors: a red chili, tomato red or whatever. And second thing is certain standard buttons we should have. Like for example, if you see the previous slide...

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Well, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: I think most of the users would now be well acquainted with this central pattern here.

transcript.speaker: William
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: So we would not change that particular pattern, because this is the most consistent thing in all remote controls.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: I can't see that, is that play and stop and things?

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
transcript.text: This is the central one, the one...

transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
transcript.text: Oh, is that volume and channel?

transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
